Below it is the confinement room, a sealed chamber close to the Sanctuary where Azar jails the Traveler. From there the Traveler wakes Nahida's consciousness with a modified Akasha Terminal.

Alhaitham's plan treats the arrest as the point: the sages would think the Traveler contained, lowering their guard. Dehya frees the Traveler later.

274.content:
Amurta (biology, green) is the Darshan of Tighnari and Naphis and runs the Bimarstan and Pardis Dhyai. Rtawahist (illuminationism, blue) was Azar's. Spantamad (elementalism, red) was Cyno's and Cyrus's. Haravatat (semiotics, black) was Khajeh's. Vahumana (aetiology, yellow) is Baladhuri's. Kshahrewar (technology, white) is Firnas's per the wiki. The Chinese names give each a descriptive name and a phonetic name; the English uses the phonetic ones.

The first Darshans were founded with the Akademiya as Six Great Schools by Rukkhadevata, each representing a type of wisdom. Others arose later but only the original six lasted. The Order of Skeptics, called Nagarjunites by the Akademiya, was once a Darshan and long ago cut its ties.

275.comment: The Akademiya: Virtues and sins of the Akademiya
275.content: The three virtues are Admonition, Ingenuity and Praxis; the six sins are listed in the governance section. They form the basis of the Akademiya's rules, to which the sages have added new rules and amendments ever since. Researching sinful topics can result in expulsion or imprisonment.

276.comment: The Akademiya: The sages' false god scheme
276.content:
Four of the six sages, led by Grand Sage Azar, agreed with Il Dottore to build a replacement god. They harvested divine knowledge from crazed scholars at a secret facility, used the Akasha to run a dream samsara, and spread false claims of King Deshret's return. Naphis and Baladhuri opposed and were locked up. Scaramouche, delivered by Dottore, was modified as the vessel.

The scheme collapsed when Nahida was freed and the Traveler defeated the made god, Shouki no Kami. The sages were removed afterwards.

277.comment: The Akademiya: The Akademiya after Chapter III
277.content: After the victory Azar and the three sages who joined him were removed, Naphis and Baladhuri were released and four new sages were to be chosen under Nahida's supervision. Alhaitham was offered Grand Sage, refused and served as Acting Grand Sage before resigning to return as Scribe, leaving the Akademiya briefly without a clear leader. By the 6.6 Archon Quest (A Divergence Leading to Oneself) Naphis is Grand Sage and introduces the new sages Alkindi (Spantamad), Firnas (Kshahrewar), Shakir (Rtawahist) and Rushd (Haravatat), alongside Baladhuri (Vahumana); when he was appointed is not shown.

278.content: A festival run by the Akademiya: Darshans set up booths around Sumeru City for the annual Wisdom Gala, and every four years each Darshan sends one representative to the Interdarshan Championship (sages may not take part). It is shown in the limited-time 3.6 event A Parade of Providence, where Kaveh (Kshahrewar) became champion over Tighnari, Faruzan, Layla, Cyno and the Wanderer.

279.content:
The Dune of Carouses (also: Dune of Carouses): The Dune of Carouses is a dune in the Hypostyle Desert of Sumeru's Great Red Sand. It is home to the Tomb of Carouses, a cone-shaped ruin that Soheil, an Akademiya researcher in Aaru Village, calls "a miniature version of the Mausoleum of King Deshret".

The tomb is the setting of the 3.1 world quest "Desert's Remembrance", part of "Soheil's Wish" in the quest chain "Old Notes and New Friends".

The Garden of Endless Pillars domain lies west of the dune. The wiki records Scarabs as the local specialty.

Geography: A dune area with the Tomb of Carouses, a pyramid-like ruin that echoes the shape of the Mausoleum of King Deshret on a smaller scale. Soheil found the same mysterious barrier keeping him out here as at his earlier ruins.

To its west is the Garden of Endless Pillars, once part of the sapphire city of Tulaytullah, where thousands of giant pillars once stood and priests and the powerful walked beneath their shade. The domain text says the garden has endured thanks to the protection of the white tree (Irminsul) and the ley lines, and is now a paradise for fungi. The wiki's exploration lists for the area include an Elemental Monument: Dendro and, in the tomb, Seelie, Forged Primal Light, Large Fan Blades, Prisms of Khaj-Nisut, Obscuring Cells and Everlight Cells.

History: Soheil's notes (days 32 to 46 of a youthful expedition) recall the day he reached the dune: "We have arrived at The Dune of Carouses." He named the cone-shaped ruin the Tomb of Carouses "for now", found it much smaller than the Mausoleum and tried to imagine how Deshret enslaved his people to build such a structure, and was turned away by the same mysterious power that blocked him elsewhere.

On the next day, the team was attacked by Eremites who called themselves Thutmose. Their two young leaders disagreed: one wanted to kill everyone, the other let them go. Soheil returned to the Akademiya feeling he had nothing to show for it. He also speculated that the Thutmose hide in rock formations, as the local sheep "disappear" near a place called Lamb-Devourer Rock. Later, in "Soheil's Wish", he sends the Traveler back to the places in his notes.

In "Desert's Remembrance" the Traveler searches the tomb; Paimon repeats Soheil's name for it, the Lesser Mausoleum of King Deshret, and notes it is a lot like the main tomb. Activating the Prism of Khaj-Nisut changes a mechanism but seems to do nothing until a switch opens a path. An Exquisite Chest holds the stone slate "Record of the Tomb of Carouses", which the Traveler can give to Soheil. In "Soheil's Wish" he studies a slate with alternating frowns and wonder, since it is his first time seeing writing like it, and he wants to visit the places where such slates were unearthed.

People: Soheil Usaibia, an Akademiya researcher found in Aaru Village, sends the Traveler on his behalf; he says he and Hulwani must patrol the area each day because young researchers keep trying to worm their way into the desert. The Eremites of Thutmose are fanatics of Deshret who once attacked his team.

Dangers: Hilichurls of several kinds (including Dendro Samachurls and shield and shooter variants), Stretchy Geo Fungi, and, inside the tomb, Primal Construct Reshapers and floating Hydro and Anemo fungi.

Atmosphere: A dune of the red desert with a small cone-shaped tomb that once turned scholars away at a barrier.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 the tomb can be entered and its slate can be given to Soheil for study; nothing else is recorded as changing.

280.comment: The Dune of Carouses: Tomb of Carouses
280.content: A cone-shaped ruin on the Dune of Carouses, a smaller echo of the Mausoleum of King Deshret. Soheil named it. A hidden barrier once kept explorers out. Inside are Primal mechanisms and a stone slate recording its history (the Record of the Tomb of Carouses).

281.comment: The Dune of Carouses: Garden of Endless Pillars
281.content: A one-time Dendro domain west of the dune, in the Hypostyle Desert. It is the surviving garden of the "city of sapphire" Tulaytullah, once dominated by thousands of giant pillars. The white tree and ley lines preserved it after the fall of the desert kingdom, and it is now a home for fungi.

282.content:
The Dune of Elusion: The Dune of Elusion is a subarea of the Hypostyle Desert in Sumeru, one of the ruins of King Deshret's civilisation. It contains the boss Algorithm of Semi-Intransient Matrix of Overseer Network.

Exploration here includes a Mysterious Mural and a Four-Leaf Sigil. The ruins south of the dune are one of the places where Primal Constructs must be defeated for the hidden exploration objective The Dead End and the Glinting Architects, which requires the quest Dual Evidence.

Geography: A desert hill with ruined structures belonging to the vanished civilisation of King Deshret, in the Hypostyle Desert of the Great Red Sand. The southernmost ruins of the Hypostyle Desert lie south of the dune.

Dangers: The Algorithm of Semi-Intransient Matrix of Overseer Network, a boss, guards the site; ruin machines called Primal Constructs are found in the ruins to its south.

Quests: The Dead End and the Glinting Architects (an unofficial wiki name for a hidden exploration objective, available after Dual Evidence).

Atmosphere: Wind-worn stone and sand over machinery older than the desert kingdoms.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 it is an explorable ruin, with nothing in the sources about later changes.

The Chinese name translates as Hill of Avoidance. The wiki lists the area as a stub, so no further points of interest or lore are established.

283.comment: The Dune of Elusion: Algorithm of Semi-Intransient Matrix of Overseer Network
283.content: This boss, a construct of the ancient desert civilisation, is found at The Dune of Elusion. See its own entry for its nature.

284.content:
The Dune of Magma: The Dune of Magma is a subarea of the Hypostyle Desert in Sumeru, a remnant of King Deshret's civilisation. It connects to the underground Rock Cavern Area at the southwest of the Mausoleum of King Deshret.

Its ruins are full of puzzle machinery: Scarlet Sand Slate puzzles (full clearance needs Clearance Level 3), a Plinth of the Secret Rites, Primal Barriers, Primal Embers, Sconces and Torches, Large Fan Blades, Verity Cells, Forged Primal Light with a Replicator Keystone, a Sacred Seal, a torch puzzle and a Time Trial Challenge.

Geography: Ruins in the red sands of the Hypostyle Desert, linked by passage to the Mausoleum's southwest rock cavern.

Dangers: Only fungi are listed as common enemies; the main hazards are the ruins' mechanisms.

Atmosphere: Ancient glowing machinery and torch-lit puzzles in sand-buried halls.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 it is an explorable ruin, with no later changes recorded in the sources.

The Chinese name translates as Hill of Melted Stone. The wiki lists the area as a stub, and no lore text, NPCs or quests are recorded for it.

285.comment: The Dune of Magma: Scarlet Sand Slate puzzles
285.content: Scarlet Sand Slate is a gadget used to solve some puzzles in these ruins; completing all of them requires Clearance Level 3.

286.content:
The Mausoleum of King Deshret (also: King Deshret's Mausoleum, Mausoleum of King Deshret): The Mausoleum of King Deshret is the huge pyramid in the Hypostyle Desert of Sumeru's Great Red Sand that has long been taken for the tomb of King Deshret (Al-Ahmar), the Lord of Deserts. For years a great cyclone turned on its summit and researchers never learned why. In the Golden Slumber quests the Traveler, Paimon and Tirzad's expedition find the way in through a mural passage in Khemenu Temple and discover that the pyramid is only one corner of a far larger palace: a mausoleum with an empty sarcophagus, an underworld-like Duat Hall, a Great Hall of Truths and, at its highest point, Aaru's Shut.

The Scarlet Sand Slate describes it as the place where King Deshret left a golden husk while his intelligence lies elsewhere, with many more temples beneath it. After Dual Evidence the cyclone is permanently gone and the summit is open.

Geography: Rises from the Hypostyle Desert in the Great Red Sand. Three levels are mapped: Main Hall, Middle Level and Lower Level. Opet Hall is an underground chamber just north; Duat Hall is reached by an underground waypoint directly south of the Mausoleum; the Great Hall of Truths connects to Duat Hall's south side; Aaru's Shut is the highest point.

A stone tablet on a plateau north-east of the Sobek Oasis waypoint in the Hypostyle Desert carries an inscription about the sandstorm and burning sun exorcising darkness and guiding the dead back to the Orchard of Pairidaeza. The Scarlet Sand Slate says the hall under the sand cannot be seen whole and craftsmen "strung natural caves with thousands of corridors", so a traveller who knows the directions will still lose their way.

Places: Entrance and Main Hall: giant doors, guardian statues and a sarcophagus chamber. Opet Hall: where blessings were said to reach the throne directly. Duat Hall: the bottomless hall, named after the Egyptian realm of the dead, where the guilty or disrespectful meet their destiny and those who pass the trials fly across an invisible river. Great Hall of Truths: where, by the slate, the wise and unafraid who bring praises to the king obtain unique gifts. Aaru's Shut: the summit.

The slate names further parts of the complex: Sekhem Hall (the source of servants who rendered the king's opponents to a handful of sand), and the three trial halls Place of Rebirth, Place of Breath and Place of Swallowing. The slate also names Abdju Road, the entrance to the king's territory, and Khemenu Temple, whose murals show Deshret's reign, as earlier stages of the journey. See their own entries.

The wiki notes that Duat is the Egyptian-derived name for the realm of the dead, the Opet in Opet Hall echoes an annual Theban festival, and "shut" in Aaru's Shut is from the Egyptian word for shadow; the Chinese name of Aaru's Shut is "Aaru's Reflection". The Mausoleum's Chinese name simply means "mausoleum of the Scarlet King". The wiki also records that Opet Hall seems to connect to the Great Hall of Truths on its south side, though players cannot cross that way and must use Duat Hall.

People: Nobody lives there. In the quests the expedition of the Akademiya researcher Tirzad, with the desert guide Jebrael and his daughter Jeht, Benben (a small Primal Construct that is evidently connected to the ruins), the Traveler and Paimon enter first. Fatui forces and Eremites, including Samail, "the Twin Blades of Thutmose", are also working in the ruins. The Vahumana researcher Soheil of the Usaibia family, who explored the desert in his youth and never found Khemenu Temple or Khaj-Nisut, later learns of the interior through Dual Evidence.

Soheil says generations of Vahumana researchers tried to open the mausoleum without success. He is accompanied by Hulwani of the Corps of Thirty, who reminds him that the sage has prohibited researchers from entering the desert without permission.

Governance: The slate's text on Opet Hall and the Mausoleum presents the king as a ruler of spectacle and devotion: the devout gain the honour of reaching the throne room, citizens travel freely and praise him, and Al-Ahmar "had no enemies" because those who paid him no homage were destroyed by servants issuing from Sekhem Hall. These are the slate's own words and reflect the king's followers' voice rather than a neutral record.

History: The building belongs to King Deshret's civilisation. Little is dated: the Record of Aaru's Shut, a stone slate left near the summit, is the fragment of a diary by someone who says Al-Ahmar made them the architect of Aaru, a project meant to protect the people after a disaster that killed the writer's father; the writer's mother blamed Al-Ahmar for the calamity in Gurabad, which the writer rejects. The writer hopes Aaru will encompass the desert, restore Gurabad and carry out Al-Ahmar's ambition, and the record breaks off when they hear a loud explosion.

Soheil explains that nearly all records of the later period of Al-Ahmar's civilisation were lost, and that even occasional finds are fragments; the Record is a perfect slate. The Golden Slumber series (3.1) shows the pyramid as part of a complex with an elevator, a hidden passage in Khemenu Temple, and three trial places that Tirzad and the slate call the king's "organs" (Rebirth, Breath, Swallowing). King Deshret himself was one of the Three Eternal Companion-Gods and died during the Archon War, according to his wiki page.

Quests: Golden Slumber (3.1), especially The Secret of Al-Ahmar: the party enters through a mural passage in Khemenu Temple, rides an elevator and reaches the Mausoleum, fights Primal Constructs, lights four Primal Torches to open a sarcophagus that proves empty, reaches the highest floor, falls into what seems to be a trap that separates the party, defeats Samail and the Fatui, and then pushes deeper into Opet Hall. Old Notes and New Friends (3.1): Dual Evidence and Soheil's Wish.

In Dual Evidence the Traveler, with the stone slate and the Ferryman's Clearance, goes through Duat Hall and the three trial places (rebirth, breath, swallowing) to the Great Hall of Truths, activates four Plinths of the Secret Rites, passes through a portal, lights three Primal Torches to activate a second device that carries them to Aaru's Shut at the top, beats a guardian construct and finds the Record. Soheil, shown the Record, says he has never seen so perfect a slate. After this the cyclone no longer turns. In Soheil's Wish, visiting the sarcophagus room afterwards, Paimon notices a hole in the floor that was not there before.

Dangers: Primal Constructs (Repulsors, Prospectors and guardians), traps that separate a party, mechanisms that need clearance, Fatui Skirmishers and Eremites in places, and Duat Hall's bottomless drop. Before Dual Evidence, the summit's cyclone made the pyramid unclimbable.

The slate's guidance for the Mausoleum warns visitors not to tarry on account of the golden vessel, to measure the buried hall by foot and not step hastily down the wrong path, and notes that thousands of corridors will confuse even a skilled navigator.

Atmosphere: Immense stone rising out of the sand, a column of wind on the roof before Dual Evidence, then corridors, murals and statues beneath. The Mausoleum is meant to make a visitor feel small. In the quests it also feels watched: doors respond to Benben, lights wake as torches are lit, and the slate speaks in short verses.

Travel: Soheil says generations of Vahumana researchers failed to open the Mausoleum; the Traveler's party succeeds with the Scarlet Sand Slate, whose clearance grows as its symbols are lit. A waypoint is unlocked at the Mausoleum and another underground, directly south of it, gives access to Duat Hall. The Old Notes and New Friends quests begin at Aaru Village.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 the Mausoleum is open to those with the slate. The cyclone is off, the summit changed, and Aaru's Shut is a permanent destination through the Great Hall of Truths.

Soheil studied the Record and counts it as a major find. In the 6.6 Archon Quest the Mausoleum and Aaru's Shut became the allies' working base during the Irminsul crisis: the Seven Pillars agreed to open Aaru, and the reconfigured Aaru has since taken over Irminsul's role of collecting and storing information. No later change to the site is shown through 7.1.

287.comment: The Mausoleum of King Deshret: Aaru's Shut and the Record
287.content:
Aaru's Shut is the highest point of the Mausoleum. The slate's description says it should have been paradise on earth and the crown jewel of the desert but now looks very different. The word Shut in the name is, according to the wiki, from the Egyptian word for shadow. At the summit the Traveler defeats a guardian construct and finds a chest with the Record of Aaru's Shut.

The Record's author, never named, calls Aaru's primary form nearly complete and promises that visitors will cross a river between the underworld and Aaru in the form of a vulture and falcon, pecking three organs and burning "embers of the sun" with feathers at three places. The text matches what the slate told the Traveler. Nothing says who wrote it beyond their self-description as the child of a fugitive and a maid.

288.comment: The Mausoleum of King Deshret: The Great Hall of Truths and Duat Hall
288.content:
Duat Hall needs Ferryman's Clearance, granted when Dual Evidence starts. It is a bottomless hall, linked to the trial places of Rebirth, Breath and Swallowing. Visitors who pass reach the Great Hall of Truths, where a giant device and four plinths open a path. According to the slate, those who bring praises before the king, who are wise and who do not fear the dark may obtain unique gifts here. A portal beyond the plinths leads to a second giant device; once its three Primal Torches (the "embers of the sun") are lit, the device lifts the party to the summit.

The three trial places promise, by the slate, an unalterable form (Rebirth), everlasting bliss (Breath) and freedom from hunger and thirst (Swallowing).

289.comment: The Mausoleum of King Deshret: Dual Evidence and Soheil's Wish
289.content: Aaru Village, after Tirzad's paper on the Golden Slumber (a study of governance in Al-Ahmar's later period), draws forty-six Akademiya students who want to enter the desert, and the Vahumana researcher Soheil is sent to turn them back. Kalantari, who asks for the Traveler's help, is the last. Soheil first dismisses Tirzad's paper, partly because the sandstorm at the top of the Mausoleum looked as he remembered it from his youth, then formally apologises, on behalf of himself and his family, once the Traveler returns with the Record. In Soheil's Wish he gives the Traveler his old archaeology notes as a "gift" so they can explore further sites for him, since the sage forbids researchers from entering the desert.

290.comment: The Mausoleum of King Deshret: The Mausoleum in the Irminsul crisis
290.content: In Song of the Welkin Moon Act IX (As All Falls to Emptiness, 6.6) the Irminsul crisis brought the Traveler, Nicole, Nefer and the Akademiya's sages and scholars into the Mausoleum, where they investigated Aaru's Shut and met Thoth, Heryshaf and Sobek. Once Nefer gave Thoth the answer "time", the three were released and, joined by Shesepankh and Bennu, with Cyno speaking for Hermanubis and Apep already aiding Nahida, the Seven Pillars agreed to open Aaru; the soul of Jebrael was among the first to emerge before it dissipated. In Act X (Truth Amongst the Pages of Purana) the Mausoleum served as the allies' base: Bennu handed Kaveh Aaru's mainframe, Kaveh and Alhaitham worked out how to override Aaru, and Nahida joined them at Aaru's Shut. After Nahida burned Irminsul, the reconfigured Aaru took over its role of collecting and storing information.

291.content:
The Orchard of Pairidaeza (also: Eternal Oasis, Orchard of Pairidaeza, Paradise of Eternal Peace): The Orchard of Pairidaeza, or Eternal Oasis, is a hidden garden beneath Mt. Damavand in the Desert of Hadramaveth, Sumeru. King Deshret built it on a divine nail as a cemetery and memorial for the Goddess of Flowers, preserving a single moment forever: animals, trees and even the water are frozen in place. It can only be entered through Deshret's Glass Goblet above it.

Desert tribes tell of it as a paradise where the slumbering goddess is guarded by Ferigees, the last mother of the Jinn. When the Traveler, Jeht and the Jinni Liloupar reach it in The Dirge of Bilqis, Liloupar finds that the goddess is not there.

Geography: Beneath the Goblet, the oasis is a still, bright garden of trees and a lake. Everything is fixed in place, including the water, which can be walked on. A central island holds three chairs, one for each of Sumeru's three god-kings, with abbreviated names written in Deshret Script. A withered Irminsul-like tree stands beside the island, which the wiki reads as showing that a Celestial Nail fell on Mt. Damavand.

Three flower buds in the garden trace trails of purple flowers; moving them through the oasis reveals memories that can be set into the three floral thrones. The Dendro Treasure Compass does not work here.

The oasis lies under Mt. Damavand, whose name in the desert dwellers' lost language means "the mountain from which smoke and ash arise"; a vast tornado whirls around the mountain's center, which the later quest Homecoming reveals to be where Apep resides. The in-game viewpoint text for the oasis quotes a verse about leaves never seized by autumn and newborn spring-joy never subject to the curse of years.

History: In a time only the Jinn could recall, King Deshret built a cemetery for his beloved, the Goddess of Flowers. With gems under the deep sands as a power source and the Jinn's help, he made an eternal oasis. Later tribes spread legends of it as ever-flourishing, ruled by the slumbering goddess and guarded by Ferigees. The Tanit, Uzza, Shimti and other matriarchal tribes call themselves Daughters of the Flower Goddess and seek the oasis for its endless knowledge.

Ferigees, once a Jinni who served Nabu Malikata, chose to serve Deshret after her mistress died, because he promised a mausoleum. She feared the consequences of Liloupar's schemes in Gurabad and gave up her Jinn body to inhabit a machine on the Goblet, guarding both the mortals and the slumber she believed was there.

Accounts: Three views of the place exist side by side. The tribes believe in a living paradise with a sleeping goddess. Ferigees believed the goddess lay in the oasis and defended it for that reason. Liloupar, after seeing it, concluded the goddess is gone and that the Lord of the Sands lied to the Jinn. The artifact text calls it a cemetery and argues that eternity is no paradise.

The artifact text imagines a conversation among Deshret, Nabu Malikata and Rukkhadevata in which one voice questions why the dunes should be commanded to stop flowing and argues that eternity is no paradise. It is a poetic scene carried by the desert winds, not a record of a real meeting.

Status as of 7.1: In The Eternal Dream, Ever Lush the equilibrium device that kept the oasis still was broken as the party entered, and the Jinni Liloupar says the oasis is destined to be buried by the sands in time. Jeht left her father's axe and her mother's notes beside a tree there.

Liloupar says the Goddess of Flowers is not there and feels no hatred, only emptiness. Jeht, a member of the Tanit tribe, finds calm in the place. Babel, the Tanit matriarch, is told of the oasis afterwards. After the Akasha Pulses quest, one throne bears Rukkhadevata's name in Deshret Script, according to the wiki (version 3.6 or later).

Atmosphere: Utterly still and bright: the air does not move, water has no ripples, and every living thing is paused mid-breath. Visitors report feeling calm and peaceful without knowing why. Beneath the peace lies a sense of loss, since the garden was made to keep something that is gone.

292.comment: The Orchard of Pairidaeza: Ferigees and the Glass Goblet
292.content: Ferigees, a Jinni who served Nabu Malikata and later King Deshret, guarded the oasis from a machine atop Deshret's Glass Goblet. She called Liloupar a traitor who had brought Gurabad down with honeyed words, refused her entry, and was destroyed when the Traveler fought her mechanical defenders. Her last words say the empty tomb will crumble. Desert legends call her the last mother of the Jinn, a gate guardian who blesses every mortal who comes to her.

293.comment: The Orchard of Pairidaeza: Jeht at the Oasis
293.content: Jeht came seeking the place her parents had spoken of. At the center of the oasis she set down her mother's notes and her father's axe beside a tree, which can be found there later. She said she might return after her adventures to lie down beside her parents' memory. Her mother's notes contain a lullaby of the eternal oasis written for her daughter.

294.content:
The Palace of Alcazarzaray (also: Palace of Alcazarzaray, Alcazarzaray): Dori asked only that it be large and extravagant, so Kaveh had almost full creative freedom. The Archive shows a purple garden before the palace where flowers dance and warblers sing. Visitors find the palace staffed by a butler, merchants and students, and people praise its architect while many do not know who owns it.

It is the setting of the start of Kaveh's Hangout Event, and Kaveh became insolvent after building it and was forced to stay with Alhaitham.

Geography: The palace stands in the Dharma Forest area of Lokapala Jungle, in the depths of the woods, just north of Sumeru City according to Dori's wiki page. A purple garden lies before it. The wiki lists Padisarah and Nilotpala Lotus as local specialties and a Four-Leaf Sigil, Auspicious Branch, Dendro Elemental Monument and bouncy mushrooms nearby.

The project site was beset by the Withering, which is why the palace is a rebuild. The grounds use ornamental plants chosen with advice from Tighnari, whom Kaveh asked for recommendations in the initial planning.

People: Dori, the owner, appears only intermittently; her butler Goshtasb says the Lord is not in and promises to introduce visitors when she returns. Other open-world figures at the palace include Gaston (a trainee reporter of The Steambird who travelled from Fontaine to interview the owner), the merchants Rajavi and Zhila, the student Sasani, and Ehsan, Mandana, Shaghayeh and Soltani. Kaveh, the architect, does not live there but still owes Dori for it.

Goshtasb says the Lord built such a big palace but no waiting place for guests at the gate. Gaston notes that everyone praises the architect but no one knows who owns the estate.

History: At some point after getting rich, Dori had Kaveh build it. Kaveh gave the project everything. Near the end of construction the Withering spread in the night, destroying the worksite and leaving it beyond saving. Dori did not want to continue, but Kaveh had already invested too much and knew how rare such an opportunity was, so he took a loan from her and rebuilt it, leaving him in massive debt (Kaveh's fourth character story).

In his voice-overs Kaveh calls it his magnum opus, says he sacrificed much for it and that others thought he had lost his mind. Tighnari says Kaveh ended up heavily in debt after it was finished and that Alhaitham lets him stay in his home. In The Price of a Wish (3.7), Kaveh insists he will repay every coin he still owes.

Atmosphere: Perfumed with jungle flowers and Padisarah, the garden is quiet apart from birdsong. A servant at the gate speaks of the Lord in formal terms; visitors wait without chairs. Wealth and a touch of absurdity sit side by side.

Quests: - The Price of a Wish (Hangout Event: Kaveh, Act I, The Pendulum of Weal and Woe, 3.7) begins here: Kaveh and the Traveler meet Dori after failing to find a sponsor for his education-and-culture project. She finally agrees to fund the project, which is aimed at giving the desert's children books, and gets Kaveh to waive his commission and shoulder the project.

The same quest reveals that Dori has been buying up land around Aaru Village; she did not tell Kaveh. During Sightseeing With Friends: Back to Sumeru, a limited-time event, Paimon points out the palace as a scenic stop for the Fungi.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 the palace is still owned by Dori and open to visitors, and no later canon changes it.

295.comment: The Palace of Alcazarzaray: Kaveh and the palace
295.content:
Kaveh, the Akademiya-trained architect known as the Light of Kshahrewar, designed the palace for Dori. He calls it his best work. The project cost him far more than it earned him, and he lives with Alhaitham because of it. Character details belong in character.kaveh.

In his voice-over about Dori, Kaveh insists he knows full well the palace is not his and does not want to discuss it further.

296.comment: The Palace of Alcazarzaray: Dori's staff and visitors
296.content: Goshtasb, the butler, defers everything to the Lord and says Dori will be in later. Gaston, a young reporter from The Steambird, wants a scoop and is certain that the owner must be someone very important. Staff call Dori Lord, and her formal title is Lord Sangemah Bay.

297.content:
The Rain's End: The Rain's End is a location in Apam Woods, in Sumeru's Dharma Forest. It is where the Traveler first gains access to the Varuna Contraption, the Aranara-tended device that sustains the rain cycle of the forest.

It unlocks during the Varuna Gatha world quests, at the end of A Prayer for Rain on the Fecund Land. Its viewpoint text says there is no rain here, yet it is the birthplace of rain, and that the purification of the Vana rains begins and ends here.

Playing the Rhythm of the Source Water on a Vintage Lyre by the contraption activates it, after which two smaller contraptions appear elsewhere in Apam Woods.

Geography: Underground in Apam Woods, in the Ashavan Realm. The southernmost contraption is found here, and it unlocks the others.

People: The Aranara Arapandu, Aranakula, Arabalika and Arakunti repair the contraption in the quest series. Its original makers are long dead, and the Nara Varuna, who once fixed it when it went wrong, is nowhere to be seen.

History: The Varuna Contraption was a device made by Greater Lord Rukkhadevata to summon timely rains in a stretch of desert, according to the original Chinese text of an item description. The English text omits this detail.

After the forest labyrinth was created, the lord of the forest Viaghara was born from the moon's reflection on the water, per Laurel Coronet text.

Quests: Varuna Gatha, including Memory of Stone, Irate Iron Chunk and Slumbering Roots, then A Prayer for Rain on the Fecund Land. Completing the series lets the Traveler change the weather in Apam Woods; this is a gameplay mechanic.

Atmosphere: Quiet, waterlogged and hushed, with the sense of a machine that lets the forest breathe.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 the contraption works and Apam Woods keeps its rain cycle; no later changes were found.

The location also holds Ragged Records, interactable notes tied to the Zandik's Legacy series; they were not read for this entry.

298.content: The Varuna Contraption controls the Varunastra, a huge pillar of water that creates the rain cycle nourishing the once-desert forest of Apam Woods. By default the weather alternates between sunny and rainy on a twelve-hour cycle, which the Traveler can override (gameplay mechanic).

299.content:
The Sands of Al-Azif (also: Sands of Al-Azif, Moonblue Canals): The Sands of Al-Azif are a comparatively flat part of the Desert of Hadramaveth in Sumeru's Great Red Sand. Wenut, the huge eyeless sand-worms of the desert, roam the surface, and the Wenut Tunnels run in the earth beneath. The City of the Deceased, a one-time domain, lies within.

The area came with the desert in version 3.4. Its viewpoint, the Moonblue Canals, preserves a desert tale that three canals once met here and watered fertile fields and rich gardens; nothing of that age remains.

Geography: One of the flatter, more open stretches of the desert, with the Wenut Tunnels, a system of caverns, below it. On the surface, Wenut rise from the sand to strike at travellers.

As a game mechanic, in parts of the Hadramaveth the Wenut erupt from the ground to attack with area blows (true physical damage), and a player can lure their strikes onto Weathered Rocks to shatter them. This is gameplay, not a separate lore claim.

The desert boss Setekh Wenut, the Last Prince of the Sands, is placed in the Wenut Tunnels (see that entry).

Places: The Wenut Tunnels (the caverns of the Wenut), the City of the Deceased domain, and the Moonblue Canals viewpoint site.

The City of the Deceased is a one-time domain whose single level is called Suspiration of the Deceased. Its in-game blurb calls them halls of death that do not welcome a flood of living things, and sends the visitor through winding corridors to clear overgrown fungi, slimes and hilichurls that should not be there.

History: Canon gives the sands no dated history. The Moonblue Canals viewpoint relays an old desert tale: this was where three canals met, feeding fields and gardens, but only the faded shade of that dream remains.

The Wenut Tunnels viewpoint adds that the mortal palaces have long fallen and the Wenut now rule there, making it a court and garden to their liking. Wenut legend (loading screens and the Setekh Wenut archive text) recalls a green age of grass and great trees that desertification ended.

Dangers: Wenut (and, in the tunnels, the boss Setekh Wenut); the fungi, slimes and hilichurls of the City of the Deceased.

Atmosphere: Scene guidance rather than canon: flat dry sand, a low hum of vibration as unseen Wenut move below, and the memory of vanished canals and palaces. The Wenut hunt by sound and vibration, so a careful traveller treads quietly.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 the sands are an open, permanent part of the Desert of Hadramaveth.

No change to the area is recorded after version 3.4.

300.comment: The Sands of Al-Azif: City of the Deceased
300.content:
A one-time domain in the Sands of Al-Azif (the wiki lists the Wenut Tunnels as its point of interest). Its single level, Suspiration of the Deceased, is a walk through winding corridors with fungi, slimes and hilichurls, and Dendro and Anemo are recommended. Its blurb: the halls of death do not welcome the deluge of living things.

The game never says whose dead the city holds or why hilichurls have taken it over; treat the identity of the deceased as unknown.

301.comment: The Sands of Al-Azif: The Moonblue Canals
301.content: Viewpoint in the Sands of Al-Azif. Ancient desert tales say this was where three canals met and nourished fertile fields and rich gardens, but only the dulled shades of a dream remain.

302.content:
The Sands of Three Canals (also: Sands of Three Canals, Land of Three Canals): The Sands of Three Canals are an elevated part of the Desert of Hadramaveth in Sumeru, north of Mt. Damavand. Desert folk still keep the name of a lost river and the green gardens that once lay here. The Fane of Panjvahe, a one-time domain, stands in it.

The area was added in version 3.4. Today the only thing the old river carries is grinding gravel.

Geography: High ground in the Great Red Sand, north of Mt. Damavand, around which sandstorms never cease.

During The Dirge of Bilqis world quest series the large Ruin Golem of the Hadramaveth is moved to a spot north of the Sands of Three Canals on its way across the desert, before it comes to rest in Wounded Shin Valley.

The golem's whole route is Dunes of Steel (where it first stands), then north of the Sands of Three Canals, then Wounded Shin Valley, where it sinks and loses its mobility.

Places: The Fane of Panjvahe, a lonesome hall where ancient mechanisms (Primal Constructs) and desert bandits (Eremites) patrol. It is a one-time domain with a single level, Fading Rumination.

The domain recommends Dendro and Electro. Its ley line disorder is a game rule that sets off Electro shockwaves when Spread or Aggravate reactions occur.

History: Loading-screen text recalls a beautiful river, navy as a moonlit night, that once flowed here in an age of songsters and flowers, marble colonnades and glazed domes. Desert people still cherish the green and blue memory and the name Three Canals; the river now carries only grinding gravel.

The name Panjvahe in the domain recalls Panjvahe, which Gurabad records describe as a long-impoverished district of that city; the wiki glosses the word as 'five oases'. Treat any link to this site as unconfirmed.

Dangers: Eremites and Primal Constructs in the fane; the open desert's sandstorms.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 the sands are an open, permanent subarea of the desert.

No change to the area is recorded after version 3.4.

303.comment: The Sands of Three Canals: Fane of Panjvahe
303.content: One-time domain in the Sands of Three Canals. The game says that when travellers step into this lonesome hall, the ancient mechanisms and desert bandits patrolling it emerge from the shadows to punish the reckless. Enemies are Primal Constructs and Eremites (Desert Clearwater, Daythunder, Crossbow and Galehunter types).

304.content:
Thinkers' Theater (also: Thinkers Theater): The Thinkers' Theater is the theatre area of the Veluriyam Mirage, the bottle-domain from the limited-time Version 3.8 event Secret Summer Paradise. Zosimos, a stage-director replica, puts on plays at its central theatre. A troupe of seven Hydro Eidolons that speaks as one voice, Daiya, stages three shows around the grounds. It was event-only.

The area unlocks with the Act III quest Treehouse Theater: Candlelit Shadows Dancing, and the world quest series Daiya's Three-Day Reverie starts here. A hidden Broadcasting Station above the central theatre opens after all three plays are completed.

Geography: Points of interest: the Central Theater (Zosimos' stage), the Director's Treehouse (where he builds props and writes scripts), an Ancient Castle in the north (always night once Petrifying Gaze is started), a Skycastle in the south, and the Broadcasting Station over the theatre. The area includes Waverider Waypoints, Dendrograna and Choo-Choo Cart track.

Zosimos' sets are built entirely from Preprints, flat blueprints made solid, so props can be moved around between scenes. The wiki lists no local specialties; enemies are Large Anemo Slimes, Winged Cryoshrooms, fungi and Hydro Mimic Mallards and Squirrels.

People: Zosimos is a moustached, Fontaine-dressed stage director, a Hydro Eidolon replica of a real prop designer who dreamed of directing. Daiya is the shared voice of seven Hydro Eidolons (Director-in-Chief, Engineer, Fake Playwright, Food Manager, Harum-Scarum, Hustler and Loafer), who talk through a device with a prerecorded vocabulary made by Zosimos and Idyia.

The seven members run the plays behind the scenes from the Broadcasting Station. Hydro Eidolons cannot speak; Zosimos taught them to direct and design shows, and Daiya is the result. The real Zosimos, according to the wiki, had aspired to direct since he was very young.

Quests: In Treehouse Theater: Candlelit Shadows Dancing, the Traveler, Klee, Kaeya and Kokomi find Zosimos in his treehouse. He holds the last component of the central hub and will give it up only after they perform his script about a thief and a mage. Klee, Kaeya and Kokomi act while the Traveler works backstage. Afterwards he gives them a bottle-lamp component and lets Klee and Kaeya keep their costumes.

Daiya's Three-Day Reverie asks the Traveler to attend three plays. The Black Nacre and the All-Devouring Kraken is a sea adventure about sailors and a hidden treasure, with cannons against a Kraken's minions. Petrifying Gaze follows a lone Hydro Eidolon breaking into a haunted fortress to lift a curse that has turned its friends to stone. Skycastle Saviors is about a floating city in crisis and its miraculous architect. Completing all three reveals the truth behind the curtain in the Broadcasting Station.

Furnishing blueprints and promotional posters are the quest rewards for the three plays, such as the Wind-Up Great Owl Spirit Mechanism blueprint for completing the series. The wiki notes that Kaveh, whom Idyia credits with redesigning many Mirage buildings, may have inspired the Miraculous Architect of Skycastle Saviors; this is inference, not stated canon.

Atmosphere: Painted flats, a speaker announcement system and an air of cheerful amateurism: a pageant staged earnestly by Hydro Eidolons.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 canon, the Thinkers' Theater is part of a time-limited area from Version 3.8; no later story returns to it.

After the event Zosimos says he has finally seen his own show, got useful feedback, and means to become a true director.

305.content: Zosimos is a Hydro Eidolon replica of a Fontaine-dressed prop designer who dreamed of directing. He is warm, grateful and open to criticism from Paimon and Idyia. His own story is a play about a thief and a mage. He calls the Hydro Eidolons dependable partners and says the outdoor stages cannot run without them.

306.comment: Thinkers' Theater: Daiya, the Seven Players
306.content: Daiya is the shared name of seven Hydro Eidolons that speak through a prerecorded-word device: Director-in-Chief (leader), Engineer, Fake Playwright, Food Manager, Harum-Scarum, Hustler and Loafer. They narrate and stage the three plays of Daiya's Three-Day Reverie.

307.content:
Tomb of Carouses (also: Lesser Mausoleum of King Deshret): The Tomb of Carouses is a small cone-shaped ruin in the Dune of Carouses, in the Great Red Sand of Sumeru's Hypostyle Desert. It looks like a scaled-down copy of the Mausoleum of King Deshret. Nobody in canon says who built it.

It is a point of interest rather than a settlement: a sealed tomb with a puzzle mechanism and a modest hoard. The scholar Soheil named it in his old expedition notes, and the Traveler later returns to it on his behalf.

Geography: The tomb stands on the Dune of Carouses within the Great Red Sand, part of the Land of Lower Setekh. The dune and its surroundings hold hilichurls and fungi, and scarabs can be gathered nearby. The tomb is a cone-shaped structure, far smaller than the Mausoleum of King Deshret.

The Dune of Carouses is a subarea of the Hypostyle Desert and also holds a Dendro Elemental Monument. Soheil's notes place the tomb on his route after the Transparent Ruins and before Lamb-Devourer Rock, on the way toward the fabled oasis he was seeking.

Places: Inside, a mechanism called a Prism of Khaj-Nisut must be activated, as in the larger Mausoleum. Doing so changes its colour but opens nothing by itself; a second switch has to be found, after which a passage is heard opening deeper in. A chest at the end holds a stone slate.

Other features recorded for the site are Seelie, Forged Primal Light, large fan blades, Obscuring and Everlight Cells, and an elite Primal Construct: Reshaper. These are the same kinds of devices met in the Mausoleum of King Deshret.

History: Its origin is unknown. When Soheil's archaeology team reached it on day 45 of his expedition, they found it shut by the same mysterious power that had kept them out of the Transparent Ruins, and he gave it its name provisionally. The next day his team was attacked by Eremites calling themselves Thutmose, led by two young men, one of whom (Samail) wanted them dead while the other (Jebrael) let them go.

Years later, in the world quest Desert's Remembrance, the Traveler and Paimon open the tomb while following Soheil's old notes. Paimon remarks that it matches Soheil's description of it as a lesser mausoleum of King Deshret and wonders which was built first; canon does not say.

Soheil, in the notes, finds it hard to imagine how Deshret enslaved his people to build the Mausoleum, and takes the same view of this smaller copy. That is Soheil's opinion in his notes, written while he was investigating, and not a settled fact.

Atmosphere: A hushed, wind-scoured sandstone cone, quiet apart from the hum of old mechanisms. It feels like a sibling of the great Mausoleum, with fewer rooms and less treasure.

Dangers: A Primal Construct: Reshaper is listed as an elite enemy at the site, and fungi and hilichurls roam the surrounding dune. Elsewhere in the desert, Eremite groups may be encountered.

Quests: Desert's Remembrance, a world quest in the Old Notes and New Friends chain that follows Soheil's Wish. The Traveler searches the tomb and brings what is found back to Soheil.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 the tomb is unchanged and open to explore. No later story involves it.

key: Record of the Tomb of Carouses
The Sheep the Bird and the Crocodile
308.comment: Tomb of Carouses: Record of the Tomb of Carouses
308.content:
A stone slate found in the tomb's chest, described as a record left by a lost civilisation. It carries a fable, The Sheep, the Bird, and the Crocodile. A sheep chief sends seven lambs to find fresh pasture; a bird, for its own reasons, sends them far north; a crocodile there pities them and escorts them home. The bird, ashamed, joins them, and on meeting the chief the crocodile devours the sheep and weeps afterwards. The moral: do not trust the meek, the wise, or those who shed tears.

The fable suggests its makers distrusted outward kindness, but who wrote it or why it was placed in the tomb is unrecorded.

309.content:
Towers of Betrayal (also: Tower of Betrayal): Those in the Hypostyle Desert, Land of Lower Setekh and Land of Upper Setekh stand on the surface but must be opened from within through the desert's cave networks. Those in the Desert of Hadramaveth are partly or fully buried and are entered at the main entrance. Each has a ground-level room with a blue crystal, and some have a basement reached by an elevator. A recorded memory of the priest Kasala, shown in Secret of the Scorching Desert, speaks of temples built by King Deshret's priests and filled with Greater Lord Rukkhadevata's power of life.

The surface towers are tied to the Hidden Exploration Objective The Three Obelisks of Necrovalley.

Geography: Towers stand in the Hypostyle Desert (northwest of the Mausoleum of King Deshret), the Land of Lower Setekh (south of Abdju Pit), the Land of Upper Setekh (west of the Valley of Dahri), and in the Desert of Hadramaveth (northwest of Khaj-Nisut, northwest of Safhe Shatranj, in Debris of Panjvahe, and in Wadi Al-Majuj).

The three surface towers are reached from underground zones: Abdju Road: Upper Ruin for Lower Setekh, Thutmose's Secret Base for Upper Setekh, and a rock cavern upper level northwest of the Mausoleum for Hypostyle Desert.

Places: - Hypostyle Desert, Lower Setekh and Upper Setekh towers: each needs Clearance level 1 to activate the crystal, open the main entrance and revive the oasis in front. Each basement holds a particle-collecting Time Trial Challenge with invisible platforms.
- Hadramaveth tower northwest of Khaj-Nisut: no accessible basement.
- Tower northwest of Safhe Shatranj: a complex Cascade Pool puzzle and the Records of the Ancient Oases Part II in the basement.
- Tower in Debris of Panjvahe: a Verity Cell puzzle with Ruins Torches on the entrance level and Part VII of the Records; a Ruin Grader in the basement.
- Tower in Wadi Al-Majuj: nothing notable; it is the setting of a fight in the World Quest For Her Judgment Reaches to the Skies... and does not play the special soundtrack of the other towers.

History: Desert tradition, quoted in the Archive, holds that the obelisks have stood since King Deshret died and shame the desert kings who broke faith with him. The Archive adds that they may be older than those short-lived kingdoms, and the real story is lost.

In Secret of the Scorching Desert, Kasala's recorded memory says that forbidden knowledge brought into the world by the Scarlet King spread like a plague, that Greater Lord Rukkhadevata summoned the priests to build temples and infused them with the power of life, and that the king finally sacrificed himself. He also says he spent his life guarding one such temple. The wiki reads the towers shown in the cutscene as these temples, which canon text does not itself confirm.

Atmosphere: Colossal stone shafts rise out of dunes or sit half-swallowed by sand. Inside is a cold chamber with a glowing blue crystal. Locals regard them with shame rather than awe, and their silence is heavy.

Dangers: Some are guarded by ruin machines or contain puzzles and invisible-platform challenges; the Hadramaveth towers lie among Eremite and Primal Construct country. Tribes consider the ruins ill-omened.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 the towers still stand, three can be reactivated by the Traveler, and no later canon changes their meaning.

310.content:
Kasala was one of King Deshret's last priests. In the cutscene Lost Legacies in the Sand, discovered in Secret of the Scorching Desert, his recorded memory describes forbidden knowledge as a plague, the priests building temples under Rukkhadevata's instruction, and the Scarlet King's self-sacrifice. He closes by urging the children of the desert to let go of old grievances and remember this kindness.

The wiki says Kasala later guarded the Mysterious Ruins, a quest-only domain, where he was entombed. Alhaitham finds his message there. That makes Kasala's guarded temple a different site from these towers.

311.comment: Towers of Betrayal: The Three Obelisks of Necrovalley
311.content: A Hidden Exploration Objective (unofficial name) about activating the three surface towers in the Hypostyle Desert, Land of Lower Setekh and Land of Upper Setekh, in any order. Each climb involves puzzles with primal light and ends in a Time Trial Challenge. Completing it grants three Precious Chests and an achievement. The towers in Hadramaveth are separate from this objective.

312.content:
Treasures Street: Treasures Street is the liveliest street in Sumeru City, one of the city's named districts alongside the Grand Bazaar and the Akademiya. It is a busy commercial strip with vendors, an Adventurers' Guild branch, Puspa Café and the Citadel of Regzar among its listed places. Its local specialty is padisarah.

Mercenaries of the Corps of Thirty, students, researchers and shopkeepers all pass through it.

Places: Places tied to the street include Puspa Café and the Citadel of Regzar, where Rukh Shah and other Corps of Thirty members are listed. Barmak, Mahamata at the Exchange, is on the roster, as are the Adventurers' Guild branch staff Kamal (branch master) and Katheryne (receptionist).

Vendors include Ahangar (blacksmith), Hamawi (general goods) and Khalid (jeweler), and Enteka runs the shop at Puspa Café. Also listed are Hassan (hairdresser, daytime), Feresht (billed as a treasure appraiser extraordinaire) and Halva (a tax officer, at night).

People: Listed street figures include Barmak, Hatim (a self-proclaimed millionaire), Mawyo (a self-described freelancer), Kimiya (a student), Mansur (a researcher), and the mercenaries Farid and Hakan of the Corps of Thirty.

At the Citadel of Regzar: Rukh Shah, Parchamdar of the Corps of Thirty; the members Sekkura ('Swallow'), Udad ('Goat') and Yunus ('Bigfish'); Asfand (a consultant) and Effendi (a researcher). At Puspa Café: Gata, Iris, Izem, Maddah, Nayab, Sanad and Zohreh, with Hatim and Mawyo at night.

Viktor appears on the street only after the quest Return to Days of Winter has been completed; nothing more is stated.

Governance: No governing body is named for the street itself. The Exchange's Mahamata, a tax officer and Corps of Thirty mercenaries work in or near it, within the Akademiya's jurisdiction over the city.

Culture: Trade and talk: sweets and padisarah, jewelry and smithing, haggling, card games and storytelling in the café, and colourful characters boasting of wealth or freelance work.

Atmosphere: Lively and crowded, with a different mix of people by day and night: a hairdresser and a freelancer by day, a tax officer and café regulars after dark.

Dangers: No dangers are described in canon.

Travel: Treasures Street lies within Sumeru City, listed with the Grand Bazaar and the Akademiya as one of its districts. The wiki lists padisarah as its only local specialty.

Status as of 7.1: Still the city's busiest street as of 7.1, as far as the sources show.

313.content: The wiki lists the Citadel of Regzar under Treasures Street. Its residents include Rukh Shah, Parchamdar of the Corps of Thirty, and members nicknamed Swallow, Goat and Bigfish. See its own entry for more.

314.content:
Tree of Dreams (also: Araja's Tree of Dreams): The Tree of Dreams is a mystic, seemingly sentient tree growing in the heart of the forest at Vanarana in Sumeru. After the cataclysm, the Aranara chief Araja turned his original body into it, so that only in its dream could the Aranara sustain a Vanarana large enough for them all.

Players unlock it with the world quest Trees and Dreams after The World of Aranara. In the Dream State it turns from green to luminous purple. Offering Dendro Sigils here raises Vanarana's Favor for rewards.

The Aranara hid the real Vanarana in a dream to protect themselves from the devastation of Sumeru; the tree is the anchor of that dream, called Mahavanaranapna by the Aranara.

Geography: Stands at the centre of Vanarana in the Dharma Forest. It looks different in the real and dream worlds: green and leafy in one, luminescent purple in the other. It is marked on the map only after it is first visited.

When Vanarana's Favor reaches its maximum, the leaves atop the tree spread open in both the real and dream versions.

People: Araja, the Aranara village chief, is the tree. His physical body can no longer move, but his mind remains intact and can manifest a body inside the dream. Over about 500 years he has lost many old memories, but he remembers taking part in the last Festival Utsava and being close to Araji, Arapacati and Aramuhukunda.

Araja tells the Traveler the story of Marana, an Aranara tale of death, and says the Aranara hid the real Vanarana in a dream after Greater Lord Rukkhadevata returned to Sarva and the rampage began. He stresses these are stories, not his memories.

History: When the original Vanarana was destroyed by the Withering in the calamity, Araja sacrificed his physical form and became the Tree of Dreams. This created the dream Vanarana, where the Aranara live in peace away from Sumeru's devastation and the harmful Nara.

The Aranara's tale of the Ashvattha Tree, planted by Rukkhadevata and the origin of the Aranara, is separate from this tree. Arama refers to a first Ashvattha's Tree of Dreams rooted in Sarva; whether it is Araja's is not stated.

Araja's story places the tree after the Cataclysm: the real Vanarana was destroyed by the Withering, the Aranara hid it in a dream, and over the last 500 years he has lost many memories. His account of Marana is explicitly told as legend, not memory.

Culture: The Aranara honour their stories and names, including those kept in the Aranyaka. Offering Dendro Sigils to the tree is the Traveler's way of earning the forest's favour.

Atmosphere: Gentle and strange: a village chief's body quietly holding a whole dream aloft, with the forest's glow shifting between green and violet as the world tips between waking and dreaming.

Quests: Trees and Dreams, a dialogue-free world quest, only shows the Traveler where the tree is. The quest begins after the Traveler speaks with Araja during The World of Aranara.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 the tree is alive and the dream Vanarana is maintained. Nothing found in 6.x or 7.0-7.1 content changes it.

315.content:
An offering system at the tree, levelled by giving Dendro Sigils in groups of 35. Before version 3.6 the maximum level was capped at 20, 30 and 40 in versions 3.0, 3.1-3.3 and 3.4-3.5. This is a gameplay mechanic.

Reaching the top level takes 1,750 Dendro Sigils and grants an achievement. Rewards include Mora, Adventure EXP and Mystic Enhancement Ore.

316.content:
Tulaytullah (also: City of Sapphire, Tulaytullah Tighnarians): Tulaytullah, the "City of Sapphire", was an ancient desert city-state in what is now the Hypostyle Desert of Sumeru. After King Deshret's civilisation fell, the priest Hermanubis brought the Tighnarians there and founded the original Temple of Silence, and the city became famed for wisdom, canals, sapphire domes and gardens. Wars among the desert kingdoms ended its glory. Only its garden is still preserved, in the Garden of Endless Pillars.

Its story is told in fragments: weapon and artifact texts, obelisk inscriptions in the Mausoleum of King Deshret, the Temple of Silence's own history, and a few quests. Legend says the city arose from the tears of Nabu Malikata after the fall of her fellow Angels. Refugees from Tulaytullah helped found Aaru Village and spread across Sumeru; some Eremite tribes and some desert-born people still trace their descent to it.

Geography: The city stood at the site of today's Garden of Endless Pillars in the Hypostyle Desert, part of the Great Red Sand. Accounts describe a lattice of shimmering canals, buildings with sapphire domes and lush emerald gardens full of padisarah flowers and pomegranates.

It was one of the Cities of the Seven Towers, the group of desert cities that Shah Ramshahr bound under his rule by raising seven towers near them, together with Ay-Khanoum and Saleh. Whether those towers are the later Towers of Betrayal is not settled.

People: Tulaytullah was home to the Tulaytullah Tighnarians, priests who had come with Hermanubis, and in later ages to an elite of nobles and scholars. Its better-known figures in the sources are King Humayun, the young noble Goudarz (later called Saleb Dowleh), the queen regent Makhaira, her lover Xiphos, the prince Faramarz and a blind poet who later led refugees to Aaru Village.

Descendants are scattered: the character Layla's blue hair and pointed ears mark her as being from Tulaytullah's line, and the Eremite tribe of the Shimti traced their ancestry to the city. The Shimti were massacred by the Iab tribe about twenty years before the present; the chief's daughter Nefer survives.

Governance: Tulaytullah's rule changed repeatedly. It was a vassal of Deshret's heirs at Gurabad and paid yearly tribute under Parvezravan; a city led by King Humayun under Shah Ramshahr; a conquered city under foreign Khagans; later a prominent state ruled by nobles and scholars, where Balash held the title of master. The elite often put its own power ahead of the people, as when it colluded with a besieging Gurabad king, and under the Khagans it treated its own citizens harshly.

History: After King Deshret sacrificed himself and his civilisation splintered, Hermanubis led the Tighnarians to Tulaytullah and set up the original Temple of Silence, which kept the knowledge that survived and held remnants of forbidden knowledge at bay. A little over a hundred years after Deshret's death war reached the desert. A Gurabad king besieged the city and demanded the Temple be handed over; the city's elite sided with him and blamed the Temple's knowledge for corruption. Hermanubis, his strength spent, broke himself into pieces and passed his power to his followers, who defeated the invaders but frightened the citizens. The Temple of Silence and the Tighnarians then left for the rainforest, and Tulaytullah fell into the wider wars.

Later events, from obelisk inscriptions: after Ramshahr died, his son Artaxir and then the Khagan Turan held the throne until Humayun and other Tulaytullah nobles rebelled, took the throne by marriage into Ramshahr's family and ruled as Humayun Gurkan. He was beheaded at Saleh in the Jinn Uprising. The warlord Makani Khagan then took Tulaytullah from a thin defence and called himself ruler of the Seven Realms; Garshasp of Ay-Khanoum later restored a fragile peace and, after his death, survivors of his burned capital fled to Tulaytullah. Goudarz, a noble who gained cunning-based kingly power from Thoth, freed the city from the Khagans, renamed himself Saleb Dowleh and went to rule at Gurabad. He allied with the port city of Orghana (now Port Ormos), and its Dey Muzaffar later killed him and his line.

In the last golden age Tulaytullah was among the desert's most prominent cities, ruled by nobles and scholars, but it came under Gurabad's king Badanah, who subjugated other cities and enslaved their people. To please him the city's elite sent Makhaira to him as a concubine. She, with Badanah's son Faramarz, killed him and passed it off as a hunting accident. A power struggle followed: Balash, Badanah's brother and Faramarz's uncle, ruled with Makhaira, Faramarz abdicated to him, and Balash was slain by another uncle, Goraz, who took Makhaira as wife. The city's nobles rebelled to avenge Balash; Makhaira appeased them with Goraz's head. Faramarz was exiled and restored three times, finally killed Makhaira with viper venom, and was ousted for the last time after a conspiracy of citizens and slave-warriors. Meanwhile Xiphos, a prince of a fallen kingdom and wielder of a blade with a Jinni in it, became the city's famed protector, the Blade of Tulaytullah. His fame earned him enemies, and the exiled Faramarz, now a mercenary, killed him for payment. Without him the city withered.

Atmosphere: In its prime, a scholarly, wealthy desert city of blue-domed halls, canals and gardens, full of scribes, priests and nobles. In its decline, a place of intrigue, conquest and betrayal, remembered by its descendants with nostalgia and caution.

Status as of 7.1: Tulaytullah is long gone. Its remembered gardens are all that remains, preserved in the Garden of Endless Pillars. It cannot be visited as a city.

Its descendants live on across Sumeru, and Aaru Village was founded by refugees from Tulaytullah and other failing desert kingdoms. As of Version 7.1 nothing found changes this.

317.comment: Tulaytullah: Hermanubis and the Temple of Silence
317.content:
Hermanubis was a Tighnarian priest who brought followers to Tulaytullah and, according to Thoth, took in many who had nowhere else to go. The Temple of Silence he founded there kept the surviving knowledge of Deshret's civilisation and, through his power, kept forbidden knowledge at bay. The Tighnarians themselves came from a place called Tighnar and had left it to serve Deshret before his death. When the city turned on the Temple, the Tighnarians withdrew to the rainforest.

Hermanubis had used up his strength by the time of the siege, which is why he broke himself apart to pass his power to his followers. The Temple of Silence's records about the siege are the main source for the event; they do not name the besieging king.

318.content: In the last age of Tulaytullah a Jinni-descended woman, Makhaira, was sent as tribute to the tyrant Badanah, and plotted with his son Faramarz to kill him. She ruled as queen regent amid constant alliances. Her first love Xiphos, the Blade of Tulaytullah, was killed by Faramarz, and Faramarz in turn ended Makhaira. Their stories survive in weapon texts and inscriptions rather than any single account.

319.comment: Tulaytullah: Aaru Village and the Refugees
319.content: Aaru Village began with refugees from Tulaytullah and other fading desert kingdoms. Among them was a blind poet from Tulaytullah who had been a general under Badanah, had known Faramarz as a child (and was blinded by him), and mentored Xiphos. Other refugees spread across Sumeru. The Shimti Eremite tribe's claim to Tulaytullah descent is recorded in the quest Dance of Death: Serpent and Scorpion.

320.content:
Tunigi Hollow: Tunigi Hollow is a subarea of Gavireh Lajavard in Sumeru's Girdle of the Sands, long a great breach carved by the Abyss. Five hundred years ago, in the cataclysm, gods fought Abyssal monsters here, and the Archon Egeria was slain. The Harvisptokhm, a tree grown from her remains, seals it.

Added in version 3.6, it is the site of the Hymn of Tir Yazad quests (Khvarena of Good and Evil). A path can be opened from the Hollow into the Harvisptokhm by the Rite of Chinvat.

Geography: A hollow, ringed by trees whose hollows hold the Great Songs of Khvarena, in Gavireh Lajavard. Gray crystal and Fravashi Trees dot it. After the Rite of Chinvat, jumping into the Hollow sends the player to the Harvisptokhm instead.

The wiki lists the nearby Dendrogranum, Elemental Monument, Farrwick and other exploration objects, and the Valley of the Unsullied viewpoint (unlocked after the Hymn of Tir Yazad, Part 1).

History: During the cataclysm, the Abyss spewed monsters and forbidden-knowledge pollution from here. Several gods ventured to suppress it, including Greater Lord Rukkhadevata and Egeria, the old Hydro Archon.

Egeria was slain and her body became the pure primordial water of the Amrita. Rukkhadevata grew the Harvisptokhm from it to anchor Egeria's consciousness and hold the Abyssal defilement at bay. The Pari fought alongside the Nagarjunites, and gray crystal encased stricken monsters for centuries.

In Sorush's vision at the top of the tree during the Hymn of Tir Yazad, Part 2, the Pari fought beside Khaenri'ahn warriors, among them a masked sword-wielder and a one-armed sage, in the cataclysm.

Places: The Harvisptokhm in the Vourukasha Oasis, reached through a hole at the Hollow or at its stump. Its heart, the Gaokerena, holds the Flower of Sanctity.

The Sign of Apaosha hangs in the sky above the Harvisptokhm. After the Hymn of Tir Yazad, Part 2 it is sealed and a tree of pure Amrita grows atop the Harvisptokhm.

Culture: The Pari treat the Harvisptokhm as their god. The Order of Skeptics once kept its seal through ritual, but lost its connection to the Pari and let the defilement build up.

The rites are the Rite of Chinvat (placing the Great Songs, which opens the path from the Hollow) and the Rite of Ab-Zohr, which purges the defilement in the tree. Mihir and Rashnu help Sorush with the Hollow's songs.

Dangers: Hilichurls, Fatui Skirmishers, rifthounds (some Thundercraven, some Rockfond), fungi, and a Consecrated Fanged Beast after the Hymn's second part. Abyssal defilement in the Hollow and tree.

Quests: In the Hymn of Tir Yazad (Part 1) the Traveler, Paimon and Sorush meet Mihir and Rashnu at the Hollow, place the Great Songs of Khvarena in the tree hollows and purify three flowers, opening the path. In Part 2 they cleanse the Harvisptokhm, collect three Spenta Hearts and awaken the god's consciousness.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 the Hollow is cleansed, with the Sign of Apaosha sealed and a clean path into the Harvisptokhm.

Before the quests the Hollow was a great breach, with its pathway blocked and the Harvisptokhm near collapse.

321.content: A rite of the Pari performed at Tunigi Hollow with the Great Songs of Khvarena. In the Hymn of Tir Yazad (Part 1), Sorush, with Mihir and Rashnu, uses it to open a pathway into the Harvisptokhm, linking the Hollow with the Sign in the sky, which loading screens call unexplained.

322.content:
Valley of Dahri: The Valley of Dahri is a wind-eroded valley in the Land of Upper Setekh, in Sumeru's Great Red Sand. A huge, sealed Ruin Golem, a war machine from Khaenri'ah (called Dahri in old Sumeru), lies in it. Scattered Akademiya research notes tell of the desert's strange hilichurl-like creatures and the Abyss.

The Valley and its golem feature in the world quest Afratu's Dilemma, added in version 3.1, in which the Traveler silences the machine's autonomous guns.

Geography: Open wind-carved country in the Land of Upper Setekh, so named because the land lies toward the sun at noon. A cavern north of the area's Statue of The Seven leads into a Ruin Golem part, and the golem itself towers over the valley.

Of the three Ruin Golems the wiki counts in Sumeru, this one is in worse repair than the Hadramaveth golem; its eye cannon can be operated freely by hand once the autonomous system is off. The viewpoint, The Giant of the Wind-Eroded Valley, appears after Afratu's Dilemma and treats the swarms from the Abyss as nearly poetic exaggeration beside such a mountain-breaking power.

Places: The Ruin Golem, and the cavern and arm passages through which one enters it, past a seal of three Suda's Flow clusters. Inside lie the cockpit and old orders written by the machine's former crew.

Notes left by Akademiya investigation teams survive in the valley. One report tells of a sage-made seal called Suda's Flow and of the hope of imitating the vein-like Vamadha seal; another says the creatures the desert folk call Majuj (hilichurls) show many traces, and that the Temple of Silence ordered every Khaenri'ahn machine sealed according to the Revelatory Monument's format.

A torn page hidden here belongs to the scholar Zandik. He writes that the golem's main guns could be repaired from abandoned parts, and that he has kept this from the rest of the team. He dismisses Suda's Flow as mere sediment from disturbed elements, absurd as the core of a seal.

People: No settlement. In Afratu's Dilemma the Vahumana Mahamata Afratu, on temporary assignment, asks adventurers to deal with the golem because the Eremites she commissioned from the Citadel of Regzar have been slow to arrive.

Afratu says Dahri is an old name for Khaenri'ah that Vahumana Darshan scholars use, and that Schwanenritter once piloted these machines against monsters from the Abyss. Three golems survived that war and were sealed by sages.

History: The golem's old orders are the main record of its past. They name a Knight Commander Hadura, honoured as Sentinel of the Golden Hall for stalling the beasts, under Marshal Regent Anfortas. Sealed orders tell the crew to abandon the machine for the Marshal's machine and to leave the wounded with supplies in a safe place, with the promise to return for them.

A badly burned medical report describes an ailment of unknown cause: peeling skin, thick hair, severe facial ulceration, impaired language, and in the first cases lost rational capacity, with patients gathered for central treatment. Nothing places the patients or the date.

An inscription at a Primal Obelisk in the valley records that Zumurud was said to have ninety-nine children, among them Badanah and Muzzudin, and that the desert kingdoms entered a golden age under them (the Gurabad wiki cites this obelisk).

Dangers: Before the quest, the golem fires beams indiscriminately at anything living near it. Inside: Ruin Guards, fungi, Dendro Samachurls, and Wooden Shieldwall Mitachurls.

Travel: The golem's guns can be baited into blasting open the rock that blocks the entrance. The scarab is the valley's local specialty.

Status as of 7.1: As of 7.1 the golem lies silent in its valley, its autonomous guns off after Afratu's Dilemma.

Afratu reported the anomaly to the Akademiya, and expects the other sealed golems to show problems if ley lines are the cause.

323.content: World quest in the Valley of Dahri. The Traveler and Paimon find the Mahamata Afratu worried about a Ruin Golem that has begun to attack. They bait it into blasting the entrance open, break the three Suda's Flow seals, and switch off its autonomous targeting from the cockpit. Vines inside suggest a ley line cause to Afratu, who passes the report to the Akademiya.

324.content:
Vanarana (also: Mahavanaranapna, Vanarana of Great Dreams, Vanarana village, Aranara village): Vanarana is the secret home of the Aranara, the small plant-like forest spirits of Sumeru's Dharma Forest. It exists twice: as a quiet clearing in the real forest, and as Mahavanaranapna ("Vanarana of Great Dreams"), a dream version where the Aranara actually live, with houses, a stage, a stall and gardens. Adults normally never find it; children and trusted friends can.

The two versions are linked by the Tree of Dreams, the elder Araja, who anchors the dream to the real world. A visitor switches between them by playing the Aranara's "Rhythm of the Great Dream" on a lyre beside a Silapna by the central pond. The village is warm, a little childlike and sentimental, and built around memories, songs and shared meals.

Vanarana is also the setting of most of the Aranyaka quest series (3.0): the Festival Utsava, the gathering of flowers from every Aranara, and the preparations for the Bija that wakes the sleeping girl Rana. Behind the village's calm lies the history of the Cataclysm, which drove the Aranara from Old Vanarana, and the lingering threat of Marana, the Withering.

Geography: Vanarana lies in the Dharma Forest of Sumeru, in the rainforest north of the desert. The wiki treats an "area" (the surroundings, including a southern stretch not touched by the dream) and a "village" proper, centred on a pond. A small garden cave at the west end grows Viparyas. In the dream version the lighting is dreamlike, a Statue of The Seven stands there, and the Tree of Dreams glows violet instead of green.

The Statue of The Seven and the cave holding the Tree of Dreams are reachable only after the opening quest, The World of Aranara; before that, the way is blocked by rock. Local plants differ between versions: Viparyas grow in the dream, while Padisarah and Nilotpala Lotus grow in the real clearing. Near the central lake the music swells and a voice joins in.

Places: Notable spots: the central pond; the Silapna east of it that toggles dream and reality; Araja's house; a festival stage; the stall of Aramani, the Aranara vendor; the nursery garden at the west end; and the Tree of Dreams in its cave.

Arama's house holds a messily written note that grows as Aranyaka advances (the writer notes new events, then Festival Utsava, then the plan to read the Aranyaka stories). The Aranara who were helped elsewhere in Sumeru (the confused, material-collecting, music-loving and reckless ones, though not the mischievous ones) later turn up in the dream village.

People: The residents are Aranara, each with a name beginning "Ara-" and each with a personal tune. Araja is the elder and village chief; Arama is the first villager to befriend the Traveler and sets them tasks to win the others' trust; Arana is a gentle Aranara tied to Rana in Vimara Village. Others include Arakavi, Arapacati, Aramani, Arakara, Aranakula, Arapandu, Aranakin and Aragaru. In total more than two dozen are named in the village.

Distinct small groups exist: song gatherers (such as Arakavi and Aradasa) who collect the tunes of other Aranara; a band that repaired the Varuna Contraption (Arapandu, Aranakula, Arabalika, Arakunti); and cooks in training around Arapacati. Aramuhukunda, the first Aranara "born", appears at the festival and later in Old Vanarana.

Governance: There is no formal government. Araja serves as chief and elder, and the Aranara decide most things together. They speak of humans as "Nara" and use "Nara" before the Traveler's name as a form of address.

Culture: Aranara cherish memories, songs and gifts of flowers (a flower given to a friend helps them be remembered). They copy human customs with no practical use: cooking although they do not eat and fear fire, houses although they do not sleep, a market although they do not trade, and the idea of siblings although they do not reproduce. Festival Utsava is their big gathering.

Their writing is the Aranara language (see its own entry). The Aranyaka book, once belonging to the earlier human friend Nara Varuna, records their stories with humans, so a person who forgets how to dream can still read of the Aranara.

History: Greater Lord Rukkhadevata created the Aranara after she left the desert to make the Dharma Forest. They first lived in Old Vanarana and befriended humans. When the Cataclysm struck they fought the invaders from the Abyss, then withdrew, set up a new Vanarana and hid it within a dream anchored by the Tree of Dreams.

Not long after the Cataclysm, Nara Varuna (named by the wiki as the Traveler's Sibling) befriended the Aranara and helped them repair the Varuna Contraption; the Aranara keep murals and monuments of this friend. After Rukkhadevata's disappearance, they remembered her as "Queen Aranyani". When Nahida (the Lesser Lord Kusanali) edited the Irminsul during the Archon Quest, the Aranara forgot Rukkhadevata in that role and now think of themselves as children of the current Dendro Archon, whom they call the Lord of Verdure.

In Aranyaka (3.0), the Traveler and Paimon reach Vanarana through the quest The World of Aranara, are tested by Arama, and gain the village's trust. Festival Utsava follows, ending with a garland from all the collected flowers. Afterwards, the Traveler and Arama take Vasoma Fruits to the weakened Fane of Ashvattha and then enter Old Vanarana to destroy Marana's Avatar; Arama becomes the new Ashvattha Tree. In the final part, Arana gives up her memory to form the Bija, which wakes Rana, who receives a Dendro Vision.

Atmosphere: Soft, dreamy and homely. Light is gentle, music drifts from the pond, and small plant-like beings fuss over cooking, flowers and festival preparations. Visitors are treated as honoured friends but the Aranara are easily frightened by humans, fire and salt. Beneath the cheer is a faint sense of what has been lost.

Dangers: The dream village itself is safe.
